newsitem.title: UK: Copper prices pull out of a dive, for now.
newsitem.headline: Copper prices pull out of a dive, for now.

text.p: Industrial metals prices stabilised on Wednesday after a sharp reverse in copper but it was gold's turn to be hit as speculators baled out in favour of a prospect of better returns in the bond market.
Gold fixed in London at $379.70 per ounce compared with $381.70 on Tuesday afternoon.
"We're getting to critical levels," a London-based dealer said. "If the pressure stays on gold it'll head down to $375..."
Talk that European central banks may sell gold as European Union countries seek to meet the 1999 single currency criteria has been depressing sentiment, dealers said.
The world price of copper stabilized and ended the afternoon session on the London Metal Exchange (LME) around $1,950 per tonne after Tuesday's dramatic $100 drop to as low as $1,916.
Traders said the metal still looked vulnerable.

The extent of selling led some to speculate that banks may still be unwinding a hoard of copper built up by Yasuo Hamanaka, the disgraced Sumitomo Corp dealer who piled up a big long position before he was fired in June as an alleged rogue trader.
Aluminium firmed in a techncial rally following copper.

Elsewhere on commodity markets, Chicago wheat futures were again little changed just below $3.85 per bushel for December against a backdrop of bumper world harvests and weaker export prospects. A surprise 1/4-point rise in British interest rates hit British grain futures. The resulting surge in value of the pound sterling against other European currencies knocked as much as 1.90 stg a tonne off wheat during the afternoon session.

Crude oil prices also eased again further from the highs of the recent brisk rally after U.S. stock data on Tuesday showed that heating oil stocks at last seemed to be building up ahead of the northern hemisphere winter.
The December contract for benchmark Brent Blend crude from the North Sea was around $23.60 per barrel late in London's afternoon from $23.75 at the same hour on Tuesday.
The American Petroleum Institute (API) said stocks of distillates (heating oil and diesel) showed a 3.6 million barrel build to nearly 118 million barrels.
Coffee, cocoa and sugar were little changed.
